subject: Smoothing in one spatial and one temporal dimension with SPDE

messages.author: d6f746729a48387e
messages.subject: Smoothing in one spatial and one temporal dimension with SPDE
parts:
I've got about 12000 observations at a 5 second frequency from some aerosol equipment that's moving back and forth across a line in space. I'm interested in fitting a spatio-temporal model to examine how the spatial trend changes with time. I managed to fit an SPDE model to the data based on the Leukemia example but I don't feel comfortable using this approach as the smoothing in space and in time shouldn't be the same (apples to oranges).

The spatial component of the data has about 2500 unique observation locations, but they're not on a regularly spaced mesh (the equipment moves back and forth with slightly different speeds each time, as it's being carried by a person). The observations are dense in both space and time and there are immobile observation points in space so we can identify spatial and temporal variation.

I've tried fitting a model using JAGS that sets up a tensor P-spline basis (Brezger and Lang, 2004) but the graph is of size tens of millions for the full data set. It segfaults on my university's supercomputer but it can run on a subset of the data (1000). The precision matrix for the prior for the spline parameters is then \lambda_1 Q_1 + \lambda_2 Q_2 where Q_1 and Q_2 are the kronecker products of the univariate smoothing penalties (as in the rw2 model) and the identity matrix.

Is there a way of using inla.spde.generic to do the appropriate smoothing so that we're smoothing in space and in time while having a mesh basis?

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Smoothing in one spatial and one temporal dimension with SPDE
parts:
Is this 2d space + 1d time or 1+1?

If its the first, it should run with the Cameletti stuff (although there'll be a limit to the resolution you can fit). If its the second, you can still use the Cameletti stuff grouping with a 1d instead of a 2d model. 

As far as I can see, the model you've proposed fits space and time the same way (with different variances), so im not sure how appropriate it is. (In maths models, the time derivative always has a different sign, so this is like fitting an anisotropic Matern model, which may well work but I'm not sure.)

For INLA.spde.generic for this model, you want to set M0=Q1, M1=0 and M2=Q2. This will fit the model
Phi1*Phi2*Q1 + Phi1*Q2,

WHere log(Phi1)=B0*THETA and log(Phi2)=B1*THETA and THETA~ N(mu,Q^{-1}). Note that this notation is a bit bad because first value of the B matrices are offsets. See the tutorials that admin has written for decent notation(sorry). For the correct values of B0 and B1 you can get your model. 

I'm a touch worried about the resolution still - 10million nodes for only 12k observations seems a bit excessive. If you want that sort of resolution, you'll have to roll your own (I don't think any existing code can touch a problem that size)

Best wishes,

Dan

Thanks Dan,

I am interested in using the Cameletti stuff in other work and have got it bookmarked.

Just checking that this is correct: Phi1*Phi2*Q1 + Phi1*Q2, multiplying the precisions together?

I am also worried about the scale of the nodes. Fitting the following model to 900 observations gives me 76448 nodes. g.prior is a vector of zeros.

model{
 for (i in 1:n){
  y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau.y)
  mu[i] <- beta.0 + gamma[i]
  gamma[i] <- X[i, ] %*% beta.s[1:K]
 }
 
 beta.s[1:K] ~ dmnorm( g.prior, lambda.1 * P1 + lambda.2 * P2)
 
 beta.0 ~ dnorm(0, tau.beta)
 tau.beta ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
 tau.y ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
 lambda.1 ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
 lambda.2 ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)

}

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Smoothing in one spatial and one temporal dimension with SPDE
parts:
On 11 October 2013 00:52, Sam Clifford <sj.cl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just checking that this is correct: Phi1*Phi2*Q1 + Phi1*Q2, multiplying the
> precisions together?

Close. Phi1 is phi0^2 and Phi2 is phi1^2 in the internal model. However:
The usual purpose of inla.spde2.generic() is to be called by wrapper
functions, but since your model doesn't have a wrapper function
(yet...) you'll need to call it directly. I've attached an example
that I think is close to what you're looking for, including a
derivation of how to translate
Q = beta.space * Q.space + beta.time * Q.time
into the internal spde2 representation

The key to remember is that even though the temporal resolution of
your data is high, the _effective_ temporal resolution at each spatial
location is given by the return-time of the measurer, so it should be
resonable to build the temporal model adapted that resolution instead
of the absolute temporal measurement resolution. The attached example
illustrates how to do that.

/Finn L

--
Finn Lindgren
